findings.title: Denial cache can persist denials computed from stale data and is never invalidated
findings.body: In Check, when the DB fallback still denies, the denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and short-circuits all later checks for that (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple. Two problems follow: (1) The deny decision may depend on the cached folder tree (checkInheritedPermissions -> buildFolderTree uses folderCache, also 30s TTL), which the DB fallback does NOT refresh. If a teammate of a folder creator checks a dashboard inside a folder created seconds ago, the fresh permission re-query returns the same scopes (e.g. only folders:uid:<grandparent>) and the stale tree has no ancestors for the new folder, so the request is denied and that deny is now cached for another 30s — extending the deny window up to ~60s after folder creation, longer than before this change, for exactly the 'newly created folder' scenario this PR is meant to fix. (2) When the fallback re-fetch does update permCache with fresh scopes, any pre-existing denial entry for a resource covered by those fresh scopes is not deleted, so the stale denial still wins over fresher permission data. Consider refreshing/invalidating the folder tree (or skipping denial caching) when the deny relied on folder-tree evaluation, and/or keying denials so a fresh allow can supersede them.

findings.title: Every denied check for a distinct resource name now triggers a full DB permission fetch
findings.body: With the new fallback, whenever the cached permission map does not contain the requested scope, Check unconditionally re-queries the full permission set from the database (getIdentityPermissions -> getUserPermissions -> permissionStore.GetUserPermissions). The denial cache only deduplicates repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parentFolder) tuple, so a caller that polls N distinct resources it cannot access (dashboard listing integrations, scanners, a user clicking through an org where most content is restricted) now issues N full permission queries per 30s window, where before this change the permission cache answered all of them with a single query per user/action. Singleflight only collapses concurrent identical user+action fetches, not sequential distinct names. Consider bounding the fallback (e.g., a short 'permissions fresh as of' marker per user/action so repeated denials on different names within a few seconds don't each hit the DB).

findings.title: Deny-cache test does not actually prove the denial cache short-circuits
findings.body: In TestService_CacheCheck/'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry', the permission cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} and the comment claims this 'allows access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope-map value of false does not allow anything, so the test returns Allowed=false even if the denial-cache logic were removed entirely: the cached perms would deny, the DB fallback (empty fakeStore) would also deny, and the assertion would still pass. To prove the denial cache is consulted, the cached value must be true — then the test would fail if the permDenialCache check in Check were removed or bypassed.

findings.title: Permission-cache hits that result in denial are recorded as cache misses
findings.body: When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed=false, execution falls out of the if-block and reaches s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...) — recording a cache miss even though the permission cache was hit. Denied checks are precisely the traffic pattern this PR optimizes, so this mislabeling systematically skews the cache hit-rate metric downward and makes the new caching behavior look less effective than it is. The hit/miss label should be recorded based on whether the cache lookup succeeded, before evaluating the allow/deny outcome.
